content.title: About
content.content: Casabe is a traditional flatbread made from cassava (manioc) root, widely consumed in the Caribbean, South America and parts of Africa. The grated cassava is pressed to remove moisture, then baked until crisp. It is gluten‑free, has a neutral flavor and can be used as a substitute for wheat bread.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Casabe has been prepared for more than 5,000 years, predating European contact.
Heat treatment destroys cyanogenic glycosides that are toxic in raw cassava.
In many regions the bread is considered a “food of the poor” because cassava grows on marginal soils.
The flatbread stays crisp for a few days but quickly softens when exposed to moisture.
Traditional recipes sometimes add coconut milk or spices to the dough.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Casabe is suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many baked goods, casabe contains virtually no fat.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Cassava provides starch that releases energy slowly.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The bread contains thiamine, niacin and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Casabe supplies potassium, magnesium and small amounts of iron.

items.title: Toxic raw cassava
items.content: Raw cassava contains cyanogenic compounds; they must be fully eliminated by proper cooking.

items.title: Low protein content
items.content: Casabe is not a significant source of protein, so it should be paired with protein‑rich foods.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to cassava.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Casabe can be eaten plain, spread with butter, avocado, cheese, or used as a base for sandwiches and tacos. It is also cut into cubes and fried to make crispy chips.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store casabe in a dry, cool place in an airtight container. For longer shelf life keep it in the refrigerator to prevent mold growth.

content.title: About
content.content: Cereal, O's, honey nut are dry whole‑grain wheat flakes enriched with honey and a nutty flavor. The flakes are light and crunchy with a sweet taste highlighted by honey and nut notes. The product is intended for a quick breakfast, usually poured with milk or a plant‑based beverage.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The original O's were launched in the 1970s as part of a major breakfast cereal line.
The honey nut variant appeared in the 1990s when demand for sweeter, aromatic cereals grew.
Flakes are coated with a thin layer of honey, giving them a characteristic golden colour.
Whole grains are retained, preserving a high amount of dietary fibre.
Packaging often features bright yellow and brown colours to emphasize honey and nuts.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Whole‑grain flakes provide sustained energy through slowly digestible carbs.

items.title: Rich in fibre
items.content: Fibre supports normal digestive function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and B6 are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Honey content
items.content: Honey adds natural antioxidants and small amounts of minerals such as potassium and magnesium.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Unlike many sweet breakfast cereals, these flakes contain minimal fat when served with plain milk.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Honey adds sugar, increasing the calorie count; people monitoring blood glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Nut allergy risk
items.content: Although the nut flavor is artificial, some batches may contain trace nuts.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Wheat‑based flakes contain gluten and are unsuitable for those with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour milk, kefir or a plant‑based drink over the flakes, wait 2‑3 minutes, then stir. They can also be added to yogurt, smoothies, used as a base for dessert parfaits, or topped with fresh fruit.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the package in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, reseal tightly to prevent moisture absorption, which can make the flakes lose their crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Maraschino cherries are preserved cherries soaked in a sweet syrup flavored with maraschino liqueur aromatics. They have a vivid red color, a sweet‑tart taste, and a distinctive aroma, commonly used in desserts, baked goods, and cocktails.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from the Italian maraschino liqueur originally used in the brining process.
Canning in syrup allows the fruit to retain its flavor and texture for several years.
The bright red hue is often achieved with food coloring, though traditional recipes use natural beet extracts.
Maraschino cherries are a staple in American cheesecake and the classic cocktail "Cherry Bomb".
Compared with fresh cherries, maraschino cherries contain significantly more sugar.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Cherries are rich in anthocyanins, which help combat free radicals.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Flavonoids may improve circulation and help lower blood pressure.

items.title: Vitamin C content
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and collagen synthesis.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Even in syrup, cherries provide some fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Cherries contain potassium, important for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The syrup makes them very sweet, which can be problematic for diabetics or those watching calorie intake.

items.title: Food additives
items.content: Some brands use artificial colors and preservatives that may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Cherry allergy
items.content: A minority of people may be allergic to cherries or to ingredients in the brine.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: The natural acidity can irritate sensitive stomachs.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Maraschino cherries are used in desserts, cakes, yogurts, ice cream, cocktails, and salads. They can be folded into batter for cupcakes or enjoyed straight as a sweet snack.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the jar tightly sealed in the refrigerator. Properly stored, maraschino cherries retain flavor for up to 12 months. Discard if mold appears or the smell changes.

content.title: About
content.content: Egg salad made with a light mayonnaise-type dressing originated in 1958. It is a classic dish where hard‑boiled eggs are mixed with a delicate, lower‑fat mayo, sometimes flavored with mustard, dill, and green onions.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The recipe became popular in post‑war America as a quick, inexpensive meal.
Light mayonnaise was developed in the 1950s as a lower‑calorie alternative to traditional mayo.
The salad is often served as a sandwich filling, on salad plates, or as a picnic snack.
The original version used only yolks, vinegar, and oil, without egg whites.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Eggs provide a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs contain B12, riboflavin, and folate, which support nervous system function and metabolism.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Light mayonnaise contains fewer fats and calories than regular mayo, making the salad more diet‑friendly.

items.title: Source of choline
items.content: Choline in yolks is important for liver health and cognitive function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Lutein and zeaxanthin in yolks help protect the eyes from age‑related changes.

items.title: Egg allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to eggs, ranging from mild to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Yolks are high in cholesterol; people with elevated cholesterol should limit intake.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Undercooked eggs can harbor Salmonella; ensure eggs are fully cooked.

items.title: Sodium level
items.content: Light mayonnaise often contains added salt; those monitoring sodium should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the egg salad cold as a snack, in sandwiches, on lettuce leaves, or as a filling for stuffed vegetables. Garnish with fresh herbs, paprika, or finely diced cucumber.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Discard if it develops an off odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: An ice cream cookie sandwich is a dessert made of two soft cookies with a scoop of ice cream sandwiched between them. Common flavors include vanilla or chocolate ice cream, and the cookies may be chocolate, vanilla, or chocolate‑chip.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first commercial ice cream sandwich appeared in the United States in the 1970s.
Cookie sandwiches are often sold in individual wrappers, making them a convenient on‑the‑go snack.
There are many filling variations: caramel, nuts, fruit sauces, and even alcoholic infusions.
Seasonal versions are popular in some countries, such as pumpkin‑spice ice cream in the fall.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: The dairy component of the ice cream provides calcium essential for bone health.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: The combination of carbohydrates and fats supplies rapid energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dairy contributes vitamins B2 and B12, supporting metabolism.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Large amounts of sugar can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of cavities.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience digestive discomfort.

items.title: Nut and gluten allergies
items.content: Some versions contain nuts or wheat‑based cookies, which can trigger allergic reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich straight from the freezer so the ice cream is soft and the cookies stay crunchy. It can be split in half for children or topped with chocolate sprinkles for extra texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen at –18 °C in the original packaging. For best quality, consume within 3–4 months; longer storage may lead to ice crystal formation.

content.title: About
content.content: Light ice cream, NFS is a low‑calorie frozen dessert made from skimmed milk, natural sweeteners, and a small amount of cream. It offers a light, creamy texture and a gentle flavor, ideal for those watching their calorie intake but still craving something sweet.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The ice cream contains about 30 % less fat than traditional versions.
The formula uses stevia‑based sweeteners, making it virtually sugar‑free.
Available in three flavors: vanilla, strawberry, and chocolate.
The product is tested to be gluten‑ and lactose‑free, suitable for most diets.
Packaging is made from recyclable plastic, reducing environmental impact.

items.title: Low calorie content
items.content: A 100 g serving provides roughly 90 kcal, allowing you to enjoy ice cream without a major energy boost.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Skimmed milk supplies a good amount of calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and supports the immune system.

items.title: Low sugar
items.content: Stevia sweeteners do not cause rapid blood‑glucose spikes.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Probiotics added to the product promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Despite the low fat, the product contains milk proteins that may trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Sensitivity to sweeteners
items.content: Some individuals may experience mild gastrointestinal discomfort from stevia.

items.title: Artificial flavorings
items.content: Certain flavors may contain additives that are unsuitable for people sensitive to food additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the ice cream at –10 °C to –12 °C. You can top it with fresh berries, nuts, or mint for extra flavor. Avoid leaving it at room temperature for more than 30 minutes to prevent ice crystal formation.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a freezer at –18 °C or lower. After opening, keep the package tightly sealed to prevent absorption of other odors. Discard the product if ice crystals form or the color changes.

pretzels-soft-from-frozen-coated-or-flav.title: Soft Pretzels, Frozen, Coated or Flavored

content.title: About
content.content: Soft pretzels are a yeast‑leavened baked snack that is produced frozen and then finished with a variety of glazes, spices or flavorings. After freezing they keep well, and a quick bake restores a warm, tender interior with a crisp, seasoned crust. They feature a slightly sweet dough base and can be coated with salt, cheese, cinnamon sugar, chocolate or other toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soft pretzels originate from Central European bakeries where they were traditionally twisted into a knot shape.
Freezing preserves the freshness of both the dough and the flavor coatings without losing texture.
More than 30 coating options exist, ranging from classic coarse salt to caramel, chili powder, and even matcha.
In the United States they are a popular bar snack, while in Japan they are sometimes glazed with soy sauce and wasabi.
The classic “8‑shape” twist ensures even baking and a uniform crust.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Pretzels provide quickly digestible carbs that supply energy for physical activity.

items.title: Contains modest protein
items.content: The yeast‑based dough contributes a small amount of plant protein useful for muscle repair.

items.title: Minerals from coatings
items.content: Salted and cheese‑based glazes add sodium and calcium, important for electrolyte balance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑enriched dough supplies B1, B2 and niacin, supporting metabolic processes.

items.title: Psychological comfort
items.content: Warm, aromatic pretzels are often associated with comfort and can improve mood.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Salty or cheese‑coated pretzels can exceed daily sodium recommendations, which is a concern for hypertension.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The dough contains wheat flour, making it unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Added sugars in sweet versions
items.content: Sugar‑based glazes increase calorie density and may raise blood glucose levels.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Soft pretzels are energy‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Bake frozen pretzels in a preheated oven at 180 °C (350 °F) for 5‑7 minutes until the crust turns golden. Serve hot, optionally sprinkling extra salt, cheese, cinnamon sugar, or drizzling with chocolate sauce. They can be enjoyed as a snack, paired with dips (cheese, mustard) or chopped into salads for added crunch.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen pretzels in an airtight bag at –18 °C (0 °F). Once thawed, consume within 2‑3 days and do not leave at room temperature for more than 4 hours. Refreezing may affect texture and quality.
